title: Suspect Zero
full_review:
A censured FBI agent must stalk an elusive killer who preys on the guilty rather than the innocent in the relentlessly dreary and generic thriller, "Suspect Zero" (Paramount).

Muddled and morose, the movie takes its title from a theory which hypothesizes the existence of a serial killer who fits no profile and follows no consistent modus operandi, making him nearly impossible to hunt.

Set in New Mexico, the film stars Aaron Eckhart as Thomas Mackelway, a headache-plagued G-man investigating a string of grisly homicides in which the victims have had their eyelids flayed and the film's ubiquitous signature symbol carved into their flesh. Six months earlier, while working for the FBI's Dallas office, Mackelway, flouting extradition laws, had engineered an unorthodox arrest which resulted in him being demoted to a bush-league branch in Albuquerque and the serial killer he collared getting off scot-free.

Consummate professional Ben Kingsley plays Benjamin O'Ryan, a creepy government-trained telepath who may or may not be responsible for the gruesome, but seemingly random, crimes.
"Suspect Zero" follows a predictable cat-and-mouse formula as Mackelway's obsession with exorcising his personal demons leads him into the very heart -- and mind -- of darkness, culminating in a, yawn, shocking revelation.

Though earnest in intent and stylishly crafted, the film's to-catch-a-killer-you-have-to-think-like-one premise is, by now, getting quite old.

Director E. Elias Merhige (whose directorial debut with "Shadow of the Vampire" was much more interesting) tries unsuccessfully to inject some intrigue by incorporating the concept of "remote viewing," the extrasensory ability to visualize what someone else is seeing and thinking -- though you don't have to be a clairvoyant to see how this one is going to end up.

The convoluted script is freighted with predictable red herrings and retread Serial Killer 101 atmospherics.

As with the cinematically superior "Silence of the Lambs" (1991) and "Seven" (1995), "Suspect Zero" is just the most recent example of packaging depravity as entertainment. Though in fairness -- apart from an unnecessarily brutal rape -- Merhige exhibits restraint in filming the lurid crimes and does not make O'Ryan into the kind of postmodern antihero that Jonathan Demme did with Hannibal Lecter.

And while Merhige has said he was initially drawn to the project because he wanted to grapple with the question of evil by exploring the dark side of human nature, the film offers little in the way of illumination. Without shedding any light, the gloomy movie simply uses human venality as an opportunity to sell popcorn.

Due to some violence, recurring grisly crime-scene images of mutilated bodies, a graphic rape with frontal nudity, as well as recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
